introduction:
Staphylococcus aureus, a gram positive, facultatively anaerobic coccus, is widely recognized for its ability to cause a broad spectrum of infections, ranging from mild skin conditions to life threatening systemic diseases [1, 2]. Commonly found as part of the commensal human microflora on the skin and in the nasal cavity, S. aureus produces distinctive golden colonies on mannitol salt agar due to mannitol fermentation [3]. The clinical significance of S. aureus increased following the introduction of penicillin; however, extensive antibiotic misuse rapidly selected for resistant strains, leading to the emergence of MRSA in the 1960s. MRSA is defined by the presence of mutant penicillin binding proteins (PBP2a) encoded by the mecA gene, which is often disseminated through horizontal gene transfer (HGT) [4, 5]. MRSA strains are commonly categorized as hospital acquired or community acquired, underscoring their major global public health impact [6].
A major factor contributing to the persistence of S. aureus infections is its ability to form biofilms. These multicellular aggregates, enclosed within a self-produced extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix, provide protection against antimicrobial agents and host immune responses, resulting in chronic and recurrent infections [7, 8]. Biofilms create a stable microenvironment that allows bacteria to withstand environmental stresses such as pH fluctuations, osmotic pressure, and nutrient limitation. Moreover, biofilm formation facilitates HGT, accelerating the spread of resistance determinants [9]. The National Institutes of Health estimate that approximately 80% of human infections involve biofilm formation [10], and bacteria within biofilms display antibiotic tolerance levels up to 1,000 times higher than planktonic cells [8]. Consequently, biofilm associated infections are difficult to eradicate, leading to prolonged hospitalization, increased healthcare costs, and elevated mortality rates [11]. The growing prevalence of multi-drug resistant (MDR) nosocomial infections has prompted the World Health Organization (WHO) to prioritize the development of novel therapeutic interventions [12].
The global escalation of AMR highlights the urgent need for alternative treatment strategies as conventional antibiotics continue to lose efficacy [13]. AMPs, also known as host defense peptides (HDPs), have emerged as promising therapeutic candidates due to their broad spectrum antimicrobial activity and distinctive mechanisms of action [14]. Typically composed of 10–50 amino acids, AMPs are positively charged under physiological conditions and contain a high proportion of hydrophobic residues, which facilitate electrostatic interactions with the negatively charged bacterial membrane [15, 16]. Upon binding, AMPs undergo structural rearrangement into amphipathic conformations that allow membrane insertion, resulting in membrane disruption, cell lysis, or interference with intracellular targets [17]. Representative examples, including nisin and magainin, demonstrate the therapeutic potential of these peptides in addressing resistant infections [16]. This review aims to synthesize current knowledge on the antibiofilm mechanisms of both natural and synthetic AMPs against MRSA. It further seeks to highlight advancements, limitations, and future directions in AMP development, emphasizing their potential as alternative or adjunctive therapies to address AMR and biofilm-associated infections.
emergence_of_mrsa:
The emergence of MRSA represents one of the most significant milestones in the history of AMR. Following the widespread introduction of penicillin in the 1940s, S. aureus rapidly developed resistance through the acquisition of plasmid-encoded β-lactamase (penicillinase), which hydrolyzes the β-lactam ring and neutralizes antibiotic activity [18]. To counter this, methicillin, a semisynthetic, penicillinase-resistant β-lactam, was introduced in 1959. However, within just a few years, resistant strains emerged, marking the origin of MRSA [3]. MRSA's resistance is primarily mediated by the mecA gene located on the staphylococcal cassette chromosome mec (SCCmec), which encodes the altered penicillin-binding protein PBP2a. This protein exhibits low affinity for most β-lactam antibiotics, thereby maintaining cell wall synthesis despite antibiotic exposure [5] shown in Fig. 1.
Mechanism of MRSA antibiotic resistance: In the presence of β-lactam antibiotics, the sensor MecR1 inactivates the repressor MecI, allowing the mecA gene to produce PBP2a, a protein that enables resistance
The global burden of MRSA infections remains profound, contributing to high mortality rates, prolonged hospital stays, and increased healthcare expenditures [19]. MRSA accounts for nearly half of all deaths associated with antibiotic-resistant bacteria [20], with annual management costs exceeding $3 billion in the United States alone [3]. Accordingly, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has recognized MRSA as a critical public health priority [3]. Clinically, MRSA infections are categorized into hospital-associated (HA-MRSA) and community-associated (CA-MRSA) types. HA-MRSA remains a persistent challenge in healthcare environments, particularly among patients with invasive devices, prolonged hospitalization, or immunocompromised conditions, leading to bloodstream, respiratory, and surgical site infections [21–23]. Conversely, CA-MRSA has emerged among individuals without prior healthcare exposure, significantly reshaping the epidemiological landscape of MRSA [24]. This strain, often carrying the lukSF-PV (pvl) genes that encode the Panton–Valentine leukocidin toxin, demonstrates increased virulence and transmissibility, frequently resulting in severe skin, soft tissue, and necrotizing infections [24–26]. Over the past two decades, CA-MRSA has surpassed its hospital-associated counterpart in prevalence, emphasizing its expanding role as a major community pathogen [3].
biofilm_formation:
Microorganisms, including pathogenic bacteria, possess the ability to attach and proliferate on both biotic and abiotic surfaces such as tooth enamel, heart valves, lungs, middle ear tissues, and medical devices [27]. This surface-associated growth leads to the development of biofilms, structured microbial communities embedded within a self-produced EPS matrix composed of polysaccharides, proteins, and extracellular DNA [28]. Biofilm formation enhances bacterial survival by promoting adhesion, structural stability, and protection from environmental stressors, immune responses, and antimicrobial agents [28]. The process of biofilm formation proceeds through five distinct but interconnected stages shown in Fig. 2: (i) reversible attachment, where bacterial cells transiently adhere to a surface via weak physicochemical interactions; (ii) irreversible attachment, mediated by adhesins such as fimbriae and lipopolysaccharides (LPS); (iii) production of EPS, where resident cells secrete structural matrix components; (iv) maturation, during which quorum sensing signaling promotes microcolony formation and three-dimensional biofilm architecture; and (v) dispersal or detachment, where bacterial cells exit the biofilm to revert to a planktonic lifestyle and colonize new sites [29].
Five stages of biofilm formation. Phase 1. Reversible attachment phase; Phase 2. Irreversible attachment phase; Phase 3. Production of EPS by the resident bacterial cells; Phase 4. Maturation phase; and Phase 5. Dispersal/detachment phase
biofilm_formation_as_a_contributory_fact:
Biofilms play a significant role in the development of AMR, posing substantial challenges in the management of bacterial infections. These structured communities of bacteria, enveloped in a self-produced extracellular matrix, exhibit complex and varied resistance mechanisms [30, 31]. They involve factors such as the protective extracellular matrix, changes in gene expression, and the emergence of persister cells, all of which contribute to the resilience of biofilms against standard antimicrobial treatments [32–34]. These mechanisms not only hinder antibiotic penetration but also enhance the survival and longevity of bacteria in unfavorable conditions [35, 36].
The formation of biofilms is a sophisticated process that commences with bacterial attachment to surfaces, followed by multiplication, maturation, and the creation of a polymeric matrix. Eventually, this leads to the detachment of microbial cells, allowing for the colonization of new surfaces [37]. Various environmental factors, including nutrient availability, temperature, pH, and the physical characteristics of surfaces, significantly influence this development [36]. Biofilms are pervasive, establishing themselves on both non-living surfaces and living tissues, and they are associated with numerous infections, particularly those related to medical devices and chronic wounds [37–39].
Several elements contribute to the increased antibiotic resistance observed in biofilms, including the shielding effect of the extracellular matrix, the presence of persister cells, and the enhanced activity of drug efflux pumps [40, 41]. Additionally, biofilms promote horizontal gene transfer, facilitating the dissemination of resistance genes among bacterial communities [42, 43]. This resistance is further complicated by the altered physiological states of bacteria within biofilms, which can lead to slowed metabolism and decreased antibiotic susceptibility [44].
To overcome the limitations posed by traditional antibiotics, researchers are exploring innovative therapeutic strategies. These strategies include the application of nanomaterials with inherent antimicrobial properties, quorum sensing inhibitors that disrupt bacterial communication, and the use of bacteriophages as targeted agents against biofilms [32, 41, 45]. Furthermore, combination therapies that incorporate antimicrobial agents, biofilm-disrupting enzymes, and immunomodulators are being investigated to improve the effectiveness of current treatments and tackle biofilm resilience [32, 36].
Thus, biofilms significantly complicate the treatment of bacterial infections due to their intricate resistance mechanisms. Achieving a thorough understanding of these mechanisms is essential for the development of targeted therapeutic interventions. Emerging approaches, such as nanotechnology and combination therapies, offer promising avenues for effectively addressing biofilm-related infections and reducing the influence of AMR [32, 36, 41, 45].
amps:
The escalating threat of AMR underscores the urgent need for alternative therapeutic strategies, as conventional antibiotics are increasingly losing efficacy [13]. Among these emerging approaches, AMPs have gained attention as promising candidates due to their broad-spectrum activity and unique mechanisms of action. These naturally occurring biomolecules, found across a wide range of organisms, typically consist of 10–50 amino acids and possess distinctive physicochemical properties that contribute to their antimicrobial potential [14]. AMPs are generally cationic under physiological conditions and contain a substantial proportion of hydrophobic residues, enabling electrostatic attraction to negatively charged microbial membranes [15, 16]. Upon binding, they often undergo conformational rearrangements into amphipathic structures that insert into cell membranes, leading to pore formation, membrane destabilization, or interference with intracellular targets [17]. Representative examples, such as nisin and magainin, exemplify the therapeutic potential of AMPs in combating MDR pathogens and highlight their relevance as viable alternatives to conventional antibiotics [16].
AMPs are a diverse group of molecules that form an essential part of the innate immune defense in a wide variety of organisms, including bacteria, plants, animals, and humans. These peptides are generally cationic and amphipathic, characteristics that enable them to interact effectively with the negatively charged membranes of pathogenic microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, viruses, and even cancer cells [46–48]. The positive charge facilitates electrostatic attraction to microbial surfaces, while the hydrophobic regions allow insertion into lipid bilayers, leading to membrane disruption and cell death. Beyond direct antimicrobial activity, AMPs can also modulate host immune responses by promoting chemotaxis, stimulating cytokine release, and enhancing wound healing [49].
AMPs can be classified into several major categories, including α-Helical, β-Sheet, loop, and extended peptides, in Table 1, we have summarized each exhibiting distinct conformations and mechanisms of action [46, 48, 50]. α-Helical AMPs typically adopt a helical conformation upon contact with membranes, leading to pore formation and membrane destabilization. β-Sheet AMPs are stabilized by disulfide bonds that enhance structural rigidity and resistance to enzymatic degradation [51]. Loop peptides contain one or more disulfide bridges that create compact and stable structures with potent antimicrobial activity, while extended peptides lack defined secondary structures and exert their effects through electrostatic interactions with microbial membranes. In Fig. 3, we have shown the structural and functional differences enable AMPs to target a broad range of pathogens, disrupt biofilms, and contribute to immune regulation, highlighting their therapeutic potential as natural and synthetic alternatives to conventional antibiotics [52].

α-Helical peptides are a prominent class of AMPs that play a critical role in combating AMR. Their unique amphipathic α-Helical structure features distinct hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions, which facilitate effective interactions with microbial membranes [46, 48]. This amphipathic configuration allows the hydrophobic face of the helix to penetrate the lipid bilayer, while the hydrophilic face interacts with the aqueous environment, leading to membrane destabilization and pore formation. For instance, representative α-Helical AMPs, such as magainins and cecropins, demonstrate potent antimicrobial activity by compromising membrane integrity and causing leakage of intracellular contents, ultimately resulting in cell lysis [53–57]. The capacity of these peptides to adopt helical structures upon microbial membrane interaction not only enhances their binding affinity but also promotes selectivity for negatively charged bacterial surfaces, making them valuable candidates in the ongoing battle against AMR.
β-Sheet peptides, particularly those found in the defensin family, are key players in the fight against AMR due to their unique structural properties and functional versatility. These peptides are characterized by stable β-Sheet configurations, reinforced by intramolecular disulfide bonds, which impart exceptional structural rigidity and resistance to proteolytic degradation [46, 48, 53]. This stability allows them to preserve their functional conformation under various physiological stresses, making them effective in diverse environments.
Defensins, encompassing both α-defensins and β-defensins, are among the most well-studied and prominent representatives of this class of peptides [46, 58]. They exhibit antimicrobial activity primarily through mechanisms that involve disrupting microbial membranes via electrostatic interactions and pore formation. This leads to the leakage of cytoplasmic contents and eventual cell death, addressing the immediate threat posed by pathogenic microorganisms. In addition to their direct microbicidal effects, β-Sheet AMPs play a significant role in modulating the host immune response, thereby enhancing overall immunity against infections. They function as signaling molecules that can induce chemotaxis, stimulate the production of cytokines and chemokines, and activate diverse immune cell types. This dual functionality enables these peptides to facilitate a bridge between innate and adaptive immunity, effectively enhancing the host's defense mechanisms [46, 58, 59].
Loop peptides are a unique category of AMPs characterized by intramolecular disulfide bonds that create compact, looped structures, enhancing their stability and resistance to enzymatic degradation [46, 53]. Notably, human defensins, particularly θ-defensins, exemplify this class and exhibit potent antimicrobial and immunomodulatory activities [46]. Their efficacy in combating AMR lies in their ability to neutralize bacterial toxins, disrupt microbial membranes, and promote immune cell recruitment and activation through chemotactic signaling pathways [46, 58]. The combination of remarkable stability and multifunctional properties positions loop peptides as promising candidates for therapeutic development against drug-resistant pathogens, offering new strategies to address the escalating challenge of AMR in clinical settings.
Extended peptides, characterized by a high abundance of specific amino acids such as proline and glycine, exhibit structural irregularity that prevents the formation of typical secondary structures like α-helices or β-Sheets [46, 60, 61]. This conformational flexibility allows these peptides to engage with intracellular targets rather than being limited to interactions with microbial membranes. Proline-rich peptides, such as apidaecin and drosocin, exemplify this category of extended AMPs [54, 61]. Unlike conventional AMPs that primarily disrupt microbial membranes, these extended peptides can penetrate bacterial cells and interact with crucial intracellular components such as ribosomes. This interaction inhibits protein synthesis, which ultimately results in bacterial cell death. Such a mechanism of action reduces the likelihood of resistance development among bacteria, as it targets essential and highly conserved cellular processes vital for bacterial survival [61, 62].
AMPs have gained considerable attention as promising agents to combat biofilm formation by MRSA. These peptides are derived from diverse biological sources and are broadly classified as either natural or synthetic. Natural AMPs originate from animals, plants, and microorganisms and exhibit multifaceted mechanisms of action, primarily involving disruption of bacterial membranes and interference with biofilm-associated signaling. For instance, [Arg]3M-PONTX-Dq3a[1–15] from Dinoponera quadriceps ant venom alters membrane permeability to inhibit biofilm formation [63]. Similarly, animal-derived peptides such as Bacitracin from Bacillus subtilis and Piscidin 1 from fish interact with bacterial membranes, compromising cell integrity and preventing biofilm establishment [64, 65]. Plant-based AMPs, including Hesperidin from citrus fruit, have also shown antibiofilm effects by downregulating biofilm-associated genes such as sarA and the ica operon, thereby attenuating MRSA virulence [66].
Synthetic AMPs, often designed based on natural templates or computational models, share common mechanisms of membrane disruption and biofilm inhibition. Designed peptides such as [G10a]-SHa, [G4a]-SHa, and [G7a]-SHa effectively interfere with bacterial membrane integrity, leading to biofilm suppression [67]. Others, including 1018M and D1018, exhibit multitarget actions, ranging from cell wall destruction to genomic DNA disruption, resulting in enhanced antibiofilm efficacy [68, 69]. Some synthetic AMPs, such as Ana-10 and CAMA, also display synergistic effects with conventional antibiotics, further improving therapeutic outcomes [70, 71]. Despite their diversity, a common mechanism among many AMPs involves direct interaction with and disruption of bacterial membranes, which compromises biofilm structural integrity. Beyond this, several AMPs modulate gene expression by downregulating critical biofilm-regulatory genes such as sarA, icaA, and icaD, thereby inhibiting extracellular matrix production and biofilm maturation [72, 73]. Others interfere with quorum sensing systems, disrupting bacterial communication and virulence regulation. However, significant gaps remain in the detailed molecular understanding of several natural peptides, including Ascaphin-8 and Lycotoxin I, whose specific mechanisms of action have not been fully characterized [65].
While in vitro studies consistently demonstrate strong antibiofilm potential, in vivo validation of many AMPs remains limited, restricting their translational applicability. Stability and toxicity also pose major challenges, particularly among synthetic peptides that may degrade rapidly or exhibit cytotoxic effects under physiological conditions. For example, D1018 has been engineered for improved stability, yet its broader pharmacokinetic and safety profiles require further assessment [69]. Furthermore, the potential development of MRSA resistance to AMPs remains insufficiently explored, posing a long-term risk to therapeutic sustainability [70]. Table 2 summarizes natural and synthetic AMPs and their roles against MRSA biofilms. Collectively, both peptide classes employ diverse yet complementary mechanisms, ranging from membrane disruption to the modulation of gene regulatory networks, to inhibit MRSA biofilm formation and persistence. By targeting pathways involved in matrix synthesis, adhesion, and quorum sensing, AMPs represent versatile tools in biofilm control. Nonetheless, future studies should prioritize elucidating the molecular mechanisms of lesser-known peptides, validating in vivo efficacy, and addressing resistance and safety concerns to fully harness AMPs as next-generation therapeutics against MRSA biofilms.

limitations_and_challenges_regarding_the:
AMPs represent a promising therapeutic approach due to their distinct mechanisms of action, which set them apart from traditional antibiotics. However, their clinical application faces significant challenges that undermine their effectiveness, particularly the emergence of bacterial resistance mechanisms and the complex architecture of biofilms. For instance, S. aureus can adapt its membrane composition by decreasing anionic lipid content, which diminishes electrostatic interactions with cationic AMPs like ATRA-1. Additionally, resistance mechanisms, such as the VraFG efflux transporter system, further limit the efficacy of these peptides [99, 100].
Biofilms further complicate the use of AMPs as they function both as physical barriers and chemical shields, impeding AMP diffusion and enhancing bacterial persistence. Within these biofilm communities, AMPs are susceptible to degradation by extracellular proteases, such as aureolysin, which is secreted by MRSA to counteract the effects of these peptides [101]. Furthermore, the biofilm matrix creates a requirement for higher concentrations of AMPs and longer exposure times to achieve bactericidal effects, especially when compared to planktonic bacterial cells [101, 102]. Therefore, addressing these limitations is essential for the effective clinical deployment of AMPs.
Some AMPs, like LL-37, have shown promise in inhibiting early biofilm formation but struggle against established biofilms, often necessitating combination therapies or the development of more potent analogs for complete eradication [103, 104]. The efficacy of various AMPs is not uniform; for example, 17BIPHE2 and WR12 demonstrate significant antibiofilm action, while L12 shows limited effectiveness even at high concentrations [80]. Despite AMPs generally having a lower propensity for resistance development, inappropriate dosing or extended exposure can still lead to the emergence of adaptive resistance mechanisms [70, 102]. Moreover, the clinical translation of AMPs is often hindered by issues of cytotoxicity and physiological instability, as seen with peptides like melittin [105]. Consequently, these challenges frequently necessitate the co-administration of AMPs with conventional antibiotics to achieve synergistic effects, complicating therapeutic regimens and dosing strategies [88].
strategies_to_enhance_the_activity_of_am:
Despite the therapeutic promise of AMPs, several challenges hinder their effectiveness against MRSA biofilms. Their susceptibility to degradation by extracellular proteases such as aureolysin reduces antimicrobial activity, and higher concentrations or prolonged exposure times are often required to achieve comparable effects against biofilm-associated cells relative to planktonic forms [101]. Nevertheless, many AMPs have demonstrated strong antibiofilm activity in both in vitro and in vivo studies, often surpassing conventional antibiotics in terms of biofilm disruption and bacterial eradication [98, 106].
The therapeutic performance of AMPs can be further enhanced through combinatorial strategies with conventional antibiotics or other bioactive molecules. Such synergy allows targeting of multiple biofilm components simultaneously, improving penetration and reducing bacterial survival [107]. Table 3 summarizes the reported synergistic interactions between AMPs and antibiotics. One notable example is the synthetic AMP L12, which exhibited synergism with vancomycin and levofloxacin, effectively reducing biofilm formation in a concentration-dependent manner, although it showed limited efficacy against mature biofilms [104]. Similarly, AMPs such as indolicidin, CAMA, and nisin enhanced the activity of antibiotics including daptomycin, linezolid, teicoplanin, ciprofloxacin, and azithromycin, resulting in marked disruption of MRSA biofilm architecture and reduction of bacterial viability. Particularly effective pairings include nisin with daptomycin or ciprofloxacin, and indolicidin with teicoplanin [71].
AMP-antibiotic combinations and their antibiofilm effects against MRSA
Additional evidence supports the synergistic potential of other peptides. The innate defense regulator peptide IDR-1018 potentiated vancomycin activity by inducing membrane perturbation and preventing biofilm regeneration [108], while melittin enhanced the activity of β-lactam antibiotics such as penicillin and oxacillin by increasing cell permeability and reducing biofilm biomass [109]. Similarly, the bacteriocin Enterocin DD14, when combined with methicillin, downregulated key virulence genes (nuc, pvl, cflA, cflB, and icaB) and inhibited biofilm formation by approximately 30% [110]. The combination of nisin with oxacillin also suppressed icaA transcription, impairing polysaccharide intercellular adhesin (PIA) synthesis essential for biofilm maturation [111]. Furthermore, α-MSH-derived peptides Ana-9 and Ana-10 exhibited strong synergistic effects with oxacillin, providing both preventive and biofilm-dispersive activity [112].
Recent progress in computational design and machine learning has significantly advanced the development of AMPs, enabling the rational prediction and optimization of sequences with enhanced antimicrobial potency and reduced cytotoxicity [113–115]. These approaches leverage extensive databases of AMP sequences and physicochemical properties to train predictive models capable of identifying novel peptide candidates and estimating their activity profiles against specific pathogens [87]. By integrating deep learning, molecular modeling, and quantitative structure–activity relationship analyses, these computational tools accelerate the design process and minimize experimental trial-and-error. As a result, several newly designed AMPs exhibit improved therapeutic indices, greater stability, and enhanced selectivity, demonstrating the potential to overcome the limitations of traditional antibiotics [57, 113, 115]. The integration of artificial intelligence and peptide engineering thus represents a paradigm shift in antimicrobial discovery, offering a data-driven framework for developing next-generation therapeutics against MDR pathogens.
Recent advances in the rational design of synthetic AMPs are transforming their potential from experimental agents into viable clinical candidates. Bioinformatics-driven approaches enable the prediction and optimization of peptide sequences with enhanced selectivity, reduced cytotoxicity, and improved resistance to enzymatic degradation [47, 50]. These computational strategies allow the fine tuning of charge distribution, hydrophobicity, and secondary structure, yielding peptides that retain antimicrobial potency while minimizing adverse host interactions. The incorporation of non-natural amino acids into AMP backbones further improves stability and bioavailability, extending their therapeutic lifespan under physiological conditions [50]. Importantly, these innovations move AMPs beyond traditional empirical discovery toward a design driven framework that integrates structure activity relationships with clinical applicability. Continued research in this direction has the potential to redefine peptide therapeutics, offering targeted and durable solutions to combat the escalating threat of antibiotic resistance across diverse infectious diseases [46, 116].
The therapeutic potential of AMPs against MRSA biofilms is often constrained by their inherent instability, susceptibility to enzymatic degradation, and limited penetration into biofilm matrices [117]. To address these challenges, advanced peptide-based delivery systems have been developed to enhance AMP bioavailability, stability, and targeted release at infection sites. These platforms, including nanoparticles, liposomes, hydrogels, and surface coatings, offer innovative approaches that protect peptides from degradation while facilitating their controlled diffusion through dense biofilm structures [118]. By improving pharmacokinetics, prolonging peptide activity, and promoting localized antimicrobial action, such delivery strategies markedly enhance AMP efficacy against persistent MRSA biofilm infections. This section discusses the most promising delivery-based systems designed to optimize AMP performance and highlights their potential applications in combating biofilm-associated MDR infections.
A variety of nanoparticle-based systems have been developed to enhance the stability, bioavailability, and targeted delivery of AMPs against MRSA biofilms. Such nanocarriers protect peptides from enzymatic degradation, improve their penetration into biofilms, and enable controlled release at infection sites [119]. For instance, a chitosan/zinc oxide (ZnO) nanocomposite loaded with the human cathelicidin peptide LL-37 exhibited strong inhibition of MRSA biofilm formation and significantly downregulated the expression of key biofilm-associated genes, demonstrating both structural and genetic disruption of the biofilm matrix [120]. In another study, diphenylalanine peptide nanotubes, particularly NH2-FF-COOH, showed potent antibiofilm activity by efficiently penetrating the biofilm matrix and disrupting bacterial cell membranes, thereby compromising biofilm integrity and viability [121]. These findings revealed the versatility of peptide-loaded nanostructures in improving peptide stability, achieving site-specific delivery, and amplifying antibiofilm efficacy against MRSA. Liposome-based formulations further complement these systems by encapsulating AMPs within phospholipid bilayers, providing an additional route for controlled release and enhanced membrane fusion at infection sites. Collectively, nanoparticle-mediated delivery platforms represent a promising strategy for maximizing the therapeutic potential of AMPs against biofilm-associated infections [122, 123].
Hydrogels have gained considerable attention as delivery platforms for AMPs owing to their excellent biocompatibility, high water content, and ability to maintain a moist environment that supports tissue regeneration and wound healing [124]. Their porous and hydrated structure enables sustained local release of encapsulated peptides directly at infection sites, enhancing therapeutic efficacy while minimizing systemic toxicity. A hydrogel pad dressing incorporating the block copolymer DA95B5 demonstrated potent antibiofilm activity in a murine wound model by effectively eliminating established MRSA biofilms. Remarkably, its therapeutic performance surpassed that of vancomycin, highlighting the capacity of hydrogel-based delivery systems to enhance localized peptide action and accelerate wound recovery [125]. This approach underscores the potential of hydrogel matrices as versatile and clinically relevant platforms for controlled AMP delivery in the treatment of chronic and biofilm-associated infections.
Coating-based delivery systems, such as catheter lock solutions, represent an effective strategy for preventing and eradicating MRSA biofilms on medical devices. These systems enable the localized and sustained release of antimicrobial agents directly at the device surface, thereby minimizing systemic exposure and reducing infection recurrence [126]. Synthetic AMPs applied through coating-based approaches have demonstrated strong activity against both early-stage and mature MRSA biofilms. Notably, the peptide Bac8c-[D-Leu2,5] exhibited remarkable efficacy in a rat central venous catheter infection model, leading to a significant reduction in biofilm biomass and bacterial load [127]. By integrating AMPs into coating or lock formulations, this method offers a practical and clinically relevant strategy for controlling biofilm-related infections associated with indwelling medical devices.
Electrospun nanofiber dressings have emerged as innovative platforms for AMP delivery owing to their high surface area, tunable porosity, and structural similarity to the extracellular matrix, which collectively facilitate controlled and sustained peptide release [128]. These nanofibrous scaffolds can be engineered to optimize drug loading, degradation rate, and moisture retention, making them ideal for wound healing applications. Notably, nanofiber dressings encapsulating the antimicrobial peptide 17BIPHE2 exhibited potent antibacterial activity against MRSA in chronic wound models, effectively eradicating biofilm-associated bacteria and promoting tissue regeneration [129]. This approach represents a promising therapeutic strategy for managing biofilm-infected wounds by combining localized AMP delivery with enhanced healing outcomes, offering a viable alternative to conventional antibiotic-based wound treatments.
enhancing_anti_biofilm_strategies_agains:
Despite the therapeutic promise of AMPs, several challenges hinder their effectiveness against MRSA biofilms. Their susceptibility to degradation by extracellular proteases such as aureolysin reduces antimicrobial activity, and higher concentrations or prolonged exposure times are often required to achieve comparable effects against biofilm-associated cells relative to planktonic forms [101]. Nevertheless, many AMPs have demonstrated strong antibiofilm activity in both in vitro and in vivo studies, often surpassing conventional antibiotics in terms of biofilm disruption and bacterial eradication [98, 106].
The therapeutic performance of AMPs can be further enhanced through combinatorial strategies with conventional antibiotics or other bioactive molecules. Such synergy allows targeting of multiple biofilm components simultaneously, improving penetration and reducing bacterial survival [107]. Table 3 summarizes the reported synergistic interactions between AMPs and antibiotics. One notable example is the synthetic AMP L12, which exhibited synergism with vancomycin and levofloxacin, effectively reducing biofilm formation in a concentration-dependent manner, although it showed limited efficacy against mature biofilms [104]. Similarly, AMPs such as indolicidin, CAMA, and nisin enhanced the activity of antibiotics including daptomycin, linezolid, teicoplanin, ciprofloxacin, and azithromycin, resulting in marked disruption of MRSA biofilm architecture and reduction of bacterial viability. Particularly effective pairings include nisin with daptomycin or ciprofloxacin, and indolicidin with teicoplanin [71].
AMP-antibiotic combinations and their antibiofilm effects against MRSA
Additional evidence supports the synergistic potential of other peptides. The innate defense regulator peptide IDR-1018 potentiated vancomycin activity by inducing membrane perturbation and preventing biofilm regeneration [108], while melittin enhanced the activity of β-lactam antibiotics such as penicillin and oxacillin by increasing cell permeability and reducing biofilm biomass [109]. Similarly, the bacteriocin Enterocin DD14, when combined with methicillin, downregulated key virulence genes (nuc, pvl, cflA, cflB, and icaB) and inhibited biofilm formation by approximately 30% [110]. The combination of nisin with oxacillin also suppressed icaA transcription, impairing polysaccharide intercellular adhesin (PIA) synthesis essential for biofilm maturation [111]. Furthermore, α-MSH-derived peptides Ana-9 and Ana-10 exhibited strong synergistic effects with oxacillin, providing both preventive and biofilm-dispersive activity [112].

Recent progress in computational design and machine learning has significantly advanced the development of AMPs, enabling the rational prediction and optimization of sequences with enhanced antimicrobial potency and reduced cytotoxicity [113–115]. These approaches leverage extensive databases of AMP sequences and physicochemical properties to train predictive models capable of identifying novel peptide candidates and estimating their activity profiles against specific pathogens [87]. By integrating deep learning, molecular modeling, and quantitative structure–activity relationship analyses, these computational tools accelerate the design process and minimize experimental trial-and-error. As a result, several newly designed AMPs exhibit improved therapeutic indices, greater stability, and enhanced selectivity, demonstrating the potential to overcome the limitations of traditional antibiotics [57, 113, 115]. challenges_in_the_clinical_translation_o:
Despite their strong antimicrobial potential, AMPs face several well-recognized limitations that collectively hinder their advancement toward clinical approval and commercial deployment. A major barrier lies in their limited stability within biological environments, where they are rapidly degraded by proteolytic enzymes, leading to a markedly shortened therapeutic lifespan and reduced in vivo efficacy [130, 131]. To address this vulnerability, numerous stabilization strategies have been explored. Chemical modifications such as glycosylation and fluorination have shown the ability to enhance resistance to enzymatic degradation while preserving, and in some cases improving, antimicrobial potency [131, 132]. However, these structural refinements often introduce new challenges by increasing the complexity and cost of peptide production, demonstrating how closely linked stability optimization is to manufacturing feasibility. Traditional solid-phase peptide synthesis remains expensive and difficult to scale, limiting the commercial potential of AMP-based therapeutics. Encouragingly, emerging technological solutions, including low-cost culture media, auto-induction systems, microbial bio-factories, and synthetic biology platforms, are beginning to address this issue by reducing production expenses and enabling more efficient large-scale manufacturing [133, 134].
Beyond these scientific and economic challenges, AMPs must also navigate stringent regulatory and commercial pathways that add further layers of complexity. Regulatory agencies require comprehensive preclinical data demonstrating not only peptide stability but also safety, pharmacokinetics, immunogenicity, and formulation robustness [135, 136]. These expectations emphasize the importance of integrating Quality by Design principles and conducting thorough pre-formulation studies early in development to facilitate a more efficient and predictable approval process [137]. From a commercial standpoint, the long-term feasibility of AMP-based therapeutics depends on successfully balancing manufacturing affordability with regulatory compliance and market readiness [138]. Moreover, the ability of AMPs to compete with traditional small-molecule antibiotics from a cost, delivery, and therapeutic standpoint will influence their acceptance in both clinical and industrial settings [139]. Advances in fermentation technologies, microbial production systems, and regulatory preparedness are therefore essential not only for overcoming existing bottlenecks but also for strengthening the future commercial viability and accessibility of AMP-based products [134, 140].
future_directives: AMPs represent a promising frontier in overcoming biofilm-associated resistance, a major factor contributing to the persistence and AMR of S. aureus, particularly MRSA. By disrupting the biofilm matrix, interfering with quorum sensing, and increasing bacterial susceptibility to treatment, AMPs offer a viable alternative to conventional antibiotics [14]. However, their therapeutic translation remains hindered by challenges such as instability under physiological conditions, proteolytic degradation, and potential cytotoxicity, which limit their in vivo efficacy. Current research is therefore directed toward enhancing AMP stability and biocompatibility through structural modifications, peptide engineering, and chemical conjugation strategies [141, 142]. The synergistic application of AMPs with conventional antibiotics has also emerged as a promising approach, as such combinations can enhance antibacterial efficacy, lower required dosages, and delay the onset of resistance. Future studies should prioritize elucidating the molecular mechanisms that govern AMP–biofilm interactions, optimizing pharmacokinetic properties, and validating therapeutic performance in clinically relevant models [107, 143]. Additionally, integrating computational design, nanotechnology-based delivery systems, and peptide optimization platforms could accelerate the development of clinically viable AMP-based therapies. Addressing these scientific and translational challenges will be pivotal in harnessing the full therapeutic potential of AMPs to combat MRSA and other MDR pathogens [144].
conclusion: AMPs represent a promising class of bioactive molecules with the potential to address the growing threat of MRSA biofilms. Their unique mechanisms, ranging from membrane disruption and interference with biofilm-associated gene expression to modulation of quorum sensing, enable them to target bacterial communities that are highly tolerant to conventional antibiotics. Both natural and synthetic AMPs have demonstrated broad-spectrum antibiofilm activity, with advances in peptide engineering, computational design, and nanotechnology further improving their efficacy and stability. Despite these advancements, challenges such as proteolytic degradation, cytotoxicity, and limited in vivo validation continue to restrict their clinical translation. Addressing these barriers through rational design, delivery optimization, and synergistic combinations with conventional antibiotics will be crucial for realizing the full therapeutic potential of AMPs. Ultimately, continued research in this field may lead to the development of safe, stable, and effective peptide-based therapeutics capable of mitigating antimicrobial resistance and improving outcomes in biofilm-associated infection.
